title: Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts
gist: Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable release (announced 12 November 2026), stabilises the never type (!) after ten years and five failed attempts, stabilises the core custom allocator API, and adds Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns (global-min-publish-age) as a supply-chain defence, with known caveats around security patching.

insights.claim: Rust 1.100.0 stabilises the never type (!), letting developers name it outside return position (e.g. Result<T, !> for operations that cannot fail), after ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Signals the Rust project can now close long-stalled language features, a maturity marker for teams weighing Rust adoption.
insights.quote: took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land
insights.locator: The headline is the stabilisation of !

insights.claim: Rust 1.100 makes std::convert::Infallible an alias for the never type, so existing APIs that use Infallible accept ! transparently.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Backward-compatible unification reduces migration friction for crate ecosystems.
insights.locator: The release also makes std::convert::Infallible an alias

insights.claim: To support the Infallible alias, Rust 1.100 ships a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping never-type fallback from () to ! (matching Rust 2024), which may cause more code to be flagged as unreachable.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Teams on older editions should update dependencies before upgrading, since fixes for widely used crates are already published.
insights.quote: largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable

insights.claim: The core of Rust's allocator_api is now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators for Vec and Box via a new Allocator trait, forming the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Opens Rust further to performance-critical and embedded/systems workloads that need allocation control.
insights.locator: The core of the long-awaited allocator_api

insights.claim: Critics on the Rust internals forum argue Rust still lacks Zig's granular allocation control because the stabilised allocator design cannot support inline storage (moves invalidate internal pointers), though the core is seen as a workable starting point.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Zig retains a differentiation niche in allocation-heavy systems programming despite Rust's progress.
insights.quote: Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation

insights.claim: Cargo's new opt-in global-min-publish-age setting holds back newly published crate versions for a configurable window (e.g. "3 days") as a defence against malicious crate releases, building the age check into dependency resolution itself rather than layering it on like GitHub's Dependabot cooldown.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Dependency cooldowns are becoming a standard software supply-chain control across package ecosystems — relevant to supply-chain security vendors.

insights.claim: Developer woodruffw argued on Hacker News that dependency cooldowns must coexist with immediate security patching, and that many tools let cooldowns obstruct urgent patches; both should be part of the resolution state machine itself.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Design tension between supply-chain delay and fast patching is an open product gap for dependency tooling.
insights.quote: you should immediately patch security advisories.

insights.claim: A beta tester found that cargo install ignores the global-min-publish-age cooldown setting entirely and that an update could downgrade a forced security fix, a caveat the release notes also flag.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The cooldown feature is not a complete defence yet; security teams should not rely on it alone.
insights.quote: an update could even downgrade a forced security fix

insights.claim: Rust 1.100 also adds core::mem::DropGuard for running a closure on every exit path, std::mem::conjure_zst for zero-sized types in unsafe code, and ergonomic APIs such as bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, str::trim_suffix and Box::map — some of which a Hacker News user noted were not even mentioned in the release blog post.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A large release scope indicates continued high velocity in the Rust standard library.
insights.quote: This release is so big that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post
insights.locator: On the Hacker News release post

insights.claim: With Rust 1.100, Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and Rust 1.101 is due around 24 December 2026 on the six-week release cadence.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Predictable cadence lets enterprises plan toolchain upgrades.
